subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Where in the periodic table are the transition metals found?
questions.explain: The transition metals occupy the central block of the periodic table between Groups 2 and 3.

questions.q: Which of these is a typical property of transition metals?
options: They have very low melting points
They are very soft and easily cut
questions.explain: Transition metals characteristically form coloured compounds and often act as catalysts.

questions.q: Why are alloys generally harder than the pure metals they are made from?
options: All the atoms are exactly the same size
Different-sized atoms distort the layers, preventing them from sliding over each other
The atoms are pushed further apart
questions.explain: Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers so they cannot slide, making the alloy harder.

questions.q: Steel is mainly an alloy of iron and which element?
questions.explain: Steel is an alloy of iron with a small, controlled amount of carbon.

questions.q: Which two substances must be present for iron to rust?
questions.explain: Rusting requires both oxygen and water to be in contact with the iron.

questions.q: What is the chemical name of rust?
questions.explain: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

questions.q: For sacrificial protection of iron to work, the protecting metal must be:
questions.explain: A more reactive metal corrodes in preference to the iron, protecting it.

questions.q: Galvanising protects iron from rusting by coating it with which metal?
questions.explain: Galvanising coats iron with zinc, which acts as both a barrier and sacrificial protection.

questions.q: Which metal would be suitable to attach to an iron pipe for sacrificial protection?
questions.explain: Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes in preference and protects the pipe.

questions.q: Which piece of apparatus is used to measure an accurate, fixed volume of solution in a titration?
questions.explain: A pipette delivers an accurate fixed volume, such as 25.0 cm3, of one solution.

questions.q: What colour is phenolphthalein indicator in an alkaline solution?
questions.explain: Phenolphthalein is pink in alkali and colourless in acid, giving a sharp end-point.

questions.q: Why is universal indicator unsuitable for use in a titration?
options: It is too expensive to use
It gives a gradual range of colours rather than a sharp end-point
It only works in acidic solutions
questions.explain: Universal indicator changes colour gradually, so there is no clear end-point to read.

questions.q: Why are only concordant titres used to calculate the mean titre?
options: They are always the largest values
They agree closely with one another, and anomalous results are excluded
They are the first results obtained
questions.explain: Concordant titres (typically within 0.10 cm3) are reliable, so anomalies are left out of the mean.

questions.q: How many moles are in 25.0 cm3 of a 0.100 mol/dm3 solution? (moles = concentration x volume in dm3)
A solution contains 0.0050 mol of solute in 0.250 dm3. What is its concentration?
questions.explain: concentration = moles/volume = 0.0050/0.250 = 0.020 mol/dm3.

questions.q: Which symbol is used to represent a reversible reaction?
questions.explain: The two half-arrows sign shows a reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a dynamic equilibrium in a closed system?
options: The rates of the forward and backward reactions are equal
All the reactants have been used up
Only the forward reaction is occurring
questions.explain: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations stay constant.

questions.q: When the temperature of a system at equilibrium is increased, in which direction does the equilibrium shift?
options: It does not shift at all
It shifts to the side with more gas molecules
questions.explain: Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat energy.

questions.q: For a gaseous equilibrium, increasing the pressure shifts the position of equilibrium towards:
options: The side with more moles of gas
The side with fewer moles of gas
Neither side, as pressure has no effect
questions.explain: Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, opposing the change.

questions.q: In the Haber process, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (forward reaction exothermic), which change would increase the yield of ammonia?
questions.explain: Higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards the 2 moles of ammonia (fewer gas molecules), increasing yield.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE (9–1) Chemistry (1CH0) specification; Separate Chemistry 1
